title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: In September Levin moved to Moscow for Kitty's confinement. He had spent a whole month in Moscow with nothing to do, when Sergey Ivanovitch, who owned property in the Kashinsky province and was very interested in the coming elections, made ready to set off there. He invited his brother — who had a vote in the Seleznevsky district — to come along. Levin also had some extremely important business to handle in Kashin to do with the wardship of land, and the collection of certain redemption money for his sister, who was abroad.

Levin was still hesitating, but Kitty, seeing he was bored in Moscow and urging him to go, took it on herself to order him the proper nobleman's uniform, costing seven pounds. And that seven pounds spent on the uniform was the chief reason he finally decided to go. He went to Kashin.…

Levin had been in Kashin six days, visiting the assembly every day and busy with his sister's business, which still dragged on. The district marshals of nobility were all caught up in the elections, and it was impossible to get the simplest thing done that depended on the court of wardship. The other matter — the payment of the sums due — kept running into snags as well. After long negotiations over the legal details, the money was finally ready to be paid out; but the notary, a most obliging man, couldn't hand over the order, because it needed the president's signature, and the president, though he hadn't formally delegated his duties, was at the elections. All this wearisome wrangling — this endless going from place to place, talking with pleasant, excellent people who fully understood the unpleasantness of the petitioner's position but were powerless to help — all this effort that produced no result left Levin with a kind of misery, akin to the mortifying helplessness one feels in dreams when one tries to use physical force. He felt it again and again while talking to his most good-natured solicitor. The solicitor really did seem to be doing everything possible, going all out to get him out of his difficulties. "I'll tell you what to try," he said more than once; "go to so-and-so and so-and-so," and the solicitor drew up a proper plan for getting around the fatal sticking point that blocked everything. But he always added straightaway, "It'll mean some delay, of course, but you might try." And Levin did try, and did go. Everyone was kind and civil, but the obstacle being skirted seemed to surface again in the end, and once more bar his way. The particularly maddening thing was that Levin couldn't make out who exactly he was up against, whose interest it was that his business should not be done. Nobody seemed to know; the solicitor certainly didn't. If Levin could have understood the reason, the way he could see why you only approach the ticket window of a railway station in single file, it wouldn't have been so vexing and tiresome. But with the obstructions in his business, no one could tell him why they existed.

But Levin had changed a good deal since his marriage; he was patient, and if he couldn't see why everything was arranged this way, he told himself that he wasn't in a position to judge without knowing the whole picture, that it must probably be so, and he tried not to fret.

At the elections too — attending them and taking part — he tried not to judge or pick fights, but to grasp as fully as he could the question that was so earnestly and ardently absorbing honest and excellent men whom he respected. Since his marriage so many new and serious sides of life had opened up to Levin, things he had once dismissed as unimportant because of his frivolous attitude, that he now assumed there must be some serious significance in the question of the elections too, and he tried to find it.

Sergey Ivanovitch explained to him the meaning and purpose of the proposed revolution in the elections. The marshal of the province, in whose hands the law placed the control of so many important public functions — the guardianship of wards (the very department giving Levin so much trouble at the moment), the management of large sums subscribed by the nobility of the province, the high schools — female, male, and military — and popular education on the new model, and finally the district council — that marshal, Snetkov, was a nobleman of the old school. He had run through an immense fortune; he was good-hearted, honest in his own way, but utterly without any grasp of the needs of modern times. He always took, in every question, the side of the nobility; he was openly opposed to the spread of popular education; and he had managed to give a purely partisan character to the district council, which by rights ought to be of immense importance. What was needed was to put in his place a fresh, capable, completely modern man with contemporary ideas, and to frame their policy so as to draw, from the rights granted to the nobles — not as nobility, but as a constituent of the district council — every power of self-government those rights could possibly yield. In the wealthy Kashinsky province, which always led the others in everything, there was now such a balance of forces that this policy, once carried through there properly, might serve as a model for other provinces — for all Russia. And so the whole question was of the greatest importance. The plan was to elect as marshal, in Snetkov's place, either Sviazhsky or, better still, Nevyedovsky — a former university professor, a man of remarkable intelligence and a great friend of Sergey Ivanovitch.

The meeting was opened by the governor, who made a speech to the nobles, urging them to elect their public officials not out of favoritism but for the service and welfare of their fatherland, and expressing the hope that the honorable nobility of the Kashinsky province would, as at every previous election, hold their duty as sacred and justify the lofty confidence of the monarch.

When he finished his speech, the governor walked out of the hall, and the noblemen noisily and eagerly — some even enthusiastically — followed him and crowded around him as he put on his fur coat and chatted amicably with the marshal of the province. Levin, anxious not to miss anything, stood there too in the crowd, and heard the governor say, "Please tell Marya Ivanovna my wife is very sorry she couldn't come to the Home." After that the nobles, in fine spirits, sorted out their fur coats and all drove off to the cathedral.

In the cathedral Levin, raising his hand like everyone else and repeating the words of the archdeacon, swore the most terrible oaths to do everything the governor had hoped they would. Church services always moved Levin, and as he spoke the words "I kiss the cross" and glanced around at the crowd of young and old men echoing the same, he felt something stir in him.

On the second and third days there was business relating to the finances of the nobility and the girls' high school — of no importance whatsoever, as Sergey Ivanovitch explained — and Levin, busy with his own affairs, didn't attend the meetings. On the fourth day there was an audit of the marshal's accounts at the high table of the marshal of the province. And then came the first skirmish between the new party and the old. The committee deputed to verify the accounts reported to the meeting that everything was in order. The marshal of the province rose, thanked the nobility for their trust, and shed tears. The nobles gave him a loud ovation and shook his hand. But at that moment a nobleman of Sergey Ivanovitch's party said he had heard the committee had not actually verified the accounts, considering such a check an insult to the marshal of the province. One member of the committee carelessly admitted this. Then a small gentleman, very young-looking but very malicious, started saying it would probably be agreeable to the marshal of the province to give an account of his expenditures of public moneys, and that the misplaced delicacy of the committee was depriving him of that moral satisfaction. Then the committee members tried to retract their admission, and Sergey Ivanovitch began to argue that they had to logically admit either that they had verified the accounts or that they hadn't, and he laid out the dilemma in detail. Sergey Ivanovitch was answered by the spokesman of the opposing party. Then Sviazhsky spoke, and then the malicious gentleman again. The discussion lasted a long time and ended in nothing. Levin was surprised they could argue over the matter for so long, especially when, on asking Sergey Ivanovitch whether he supposed money had been misappropriated, Sergey Ivanovitch answered:
"Oh, no! He's an honest man. But those old-fashioned paternal-family methods of running provincial affairs have to be broken down."

On the fifth day the elections of the district marshals took place. It was a fairly stormy day in several districts. In the Seleznevsky district Sviazhsky was elected unanimously, without a ballot, and he gave a dinner that evening.
